analysis.one_liner: Lets owners of contaminated Superfund sites clean up voluntarily and get legal protection from future lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees in July 1993, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary cleanup track for sites on the federal Superfund list and state hazardous-site lists. An owner or operator could notify the EPA of intent to clean up, pay the agency's oversight costs plus a $5,000 fee, post a bond, and submit a public investigation and cleanup plan. Once the work was certified complete, the EPA would have to sign a covenant not to sue the owner or other responsible parties for Superfund liability and remove the site from the national priorities list.
analysis.who_benefits: Two groups gain. Owners and operators of contaminated sites, and other parties held responsible for the pollution, gain certainty: they pay for the cleanup and oversight, but in exchange they are released from the open-ended liability that Superfund otherwise imposes. Communities living near contaminated sites also stand to gain, because sites that might sit for years under the standard EPA-run process could be cleaned up faster and redeveloped, with the investigation results and cleanup plans open to public review.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Polluters cleaning sites, and nearby communities

how_it_helps.text: Owners pay 100% of cleanup costs plus 100% of the EPA's documented oversight costs, and must post a bond ensuring the cleanup is finished [S3].
Facility investigation results must be available to the public, and cleanup and redevelopment plans go through published notice and a 30-day public comment period [S3].
States may run the program if they guarantee public participation, technical assistance, oversight and enforcement authority, and cleanup responsibility if the owner fails to finish [S3].

After certification of completion, the EPA must enter a covenant not to sue and remove the site from the National Priorities List, ending years of liability uncertainty that often keeps contaminated land idle [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Nearby residents and the public bear the risk side of the bargain: the covenant not to sue wipes out civil Superfund claims against the polluting parties, the cleanup standard is loosened to account for a site's planned future use rather than full restoration, and performance under the program could not be used as evidence in citizen lawsuits. Taxpayers also give up any recovery beyond the documented oversight costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near sites, via weaker standards

drawbacks.text: Upon certification of completion, the EPA must sign a covenant not to sue the owner, operator, and any other responsible parties for civil Superfund liability, and remove the site from the National Priorities List — trading away the government's main enforcement leverage [S2].

The bill amends CERCLA so the required cleanup level is whatever the administrator deems appropriate, taking into account the site's planned redevelopment, expected exposure, and migration risk — meaning sites slated for industrial reuse could be cleaned to a lower standard than full restoration [S3].
Cleanup work done under the program could not be admitted as evidence in citizen suits or private actions, and disputes over cost reimbursement go to arbitration rather than court [S3].

The EPA must approve or disapprove a completed cleanup within 135 days or the owner can go to court to force a decision, and the agency can require additional work only under a short list of specified circumstances — for example, newly discovered public health risks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real benefit: Superfund cleanups have historically dragged on for years amid litigation over who pays, and a voluntary track with public participation could get sites cleaned and back in use faster. But the price is substantial: polluting companies get a legally binding release from future Superfund claims once they certify completion, and the cleanup target is set partly by what the owner plans to do with the land afterward. Whether that trade favors the public depends on rigorous oversight — exactly the thing the bill's tight deadlines and narrow grounds for ordering more work make harder to enforce.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees for a year with no hearing or vote; in July 1994 the record closed it out by pointing to a related bill, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kreidler introduced the bill on July 22, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Public Works + Transportation committees [S5].
In August 1993 it was sent to subcommittees in each committee — Water Resources and Environment, and Transportation and Hazardous Materials — where no action followed [S5].
On July 27, 1994, the House action history recorded only 'See H.R.3800', a reference to a related bill; H.R. 2709 itself never received a vote [S5].
The bill attracted four cosponsors, two Democrats and two Republicans, but that support never translated into committee or floor action before the 103rd Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held. Companies responsible for contaminated sites kept facing open-ended Superfund liability, but the EPA also kept its full enforcement leverage, and communities near contaminated sites continued waiting on the slower, litigation-heavy standard cleanup process that this bill was meant to bypass.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: no faster cleanups, no liability release

industries.industry: Owners and operators of contaminated sites (chemical, manufacturing, and other Superfund responsible parties)
industries.note: The bill would give these companies a covenant not to sue and removal from the Superfund list once they finish an approved cleanup — ending their biggest source of uncertainty. Their interest cuts both ways for the public: they must pay the full cleanup and oversight costs, but the liability release and reuse-based cleanup standards also mean potentially less thorough remediation.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and brownfield redevelopers
industries.note: A certified cleanup with a covenant not to sue makes contaminated land legally usable again, opening sites that liability risk currently keeps idle. Redevelopment plans could even be written into the approved cleanup plan.
A voluntary cleanup track creates paid work for the engineers and contractors who conduct the investigations, remediations, and monitoring the bill requires.
The bill requires owners to secure a bond guaranteeing cleanup completion, generating surety business — with the premium cost ultimately borne by the site owner.
